about: ENGF0035 is the Year 1 Electronic and Electrical Engineering version of the Design and Professional Skills strand of UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme, with a Part II in Year 2. UCL's IEP pages describe a multi-year syllabus covering ethics, professional standards, sustainability, communication, risk and safety, critical and creative thinking, decision making, design and teamwork, taught through design and professional practice workshops alongside intensive team scenario weeks. The module's catalogue page could not be read when this pack was written, so its credits, term and assessment are not given here; check the current catalogue entry and Moodle. This guide covers the standard planning, decision-making and writing tools such projects use, rather than a fixed syllabus.

notes.body:
Design and Professional Skills I (Electronic and Electrical Engineering), ENGF0035, is the Year 1 Electronic and Electrical Engineering version of the Design and Professional Skills strand of UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme (IEP). Each IEP department runs its own version of the module, and a Part II follows in Year 2.

What UCL's IEP pages say about it
- It belongs to a multi-year syllabus covering ethics, professional standards, sustainability, legal and management concepts, communication, risk and safety, creative and critical thinking, decision making, design and teamwork.
- Design is treated as the place where these skills are applied, so the module is closely linked to the practical work.
- It is delivered through design and professional practice workshops aligned with the programme's practical activities.
- It runs alongside the IEP's scenario weeks: intensive team projects, kept separate from the rest of the timetable, in which you apply taught material to an engineering problem across the design cycle, from capturing requirements to building and testing.

What we could not confirm
- The module's own catalogue page could not be read when this pack was written, so its credit value, teaching term(s) and assessment pattern are not given here. Check the current UCL module catalogue entry for ENGF0035 and your Moodle page for these details.
- The specific scenario-week briefs for Electronic and Electrical Engineering are set by the department each year and are not published in advance.

How to approach it
- Treat each workshop as practice for the next scenario: the planning tools, decision methods and writing skills are what you will be marked on using.
- Keep a project log or shared folder for every team project: meeting notes, decisions and the reasons for them, versions of your plan and risk register, test results. These make the final report and any reflection much easier to write.
- Learn the small set of standard tools in this pack (Gantt charts, risk registers, weighted decision matrices, report structure) well enough to use them quickly under time pressure.
- Read briefs carefully: identify the deliverables, deadlines, constraints and marking criteria before starting design work.

notes.h: Project planning: Gantt charts and risk registers
notes.body:
Scenario weeks are short, so planning is part of what makes a team succeed. Two standard tools appear in almost every engineering project.

Gantt charts
- A bar chart with tasks listed down the side and time along the bottom; each bar shows when a task starts and ends.
- Show dependencies (task B cannot start until task A finishes), milestones (zero-length checkpoints such as "prototype working" or "report submitted", usually drawn as diamonds) and who owns each task.
- The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks through the project; it fixes the shortest possible project duration. Any delay to a critical task delays the whole project.
- Float (slack) is how long a non-critical task can slip without delaying the end date.
- Worked example: A (3 days); B (2 days, after A); C (4 days, after A); D (2 days, after both B and C). Path A–B–D takes 7 days, path A–C–D takes 9 days, so the critical path is A–C–D and the project takes 9 days. B has 2 days of float.
- Good practice: break work into tasks small enough to estimate (hours or days, not "build the circuit"), allow time for integration and testing, and update the chart as things change.

Risk registers
- A table listing each identified risk with: a description (cause and effect), likelihood, impact, a risk score, the planned response, an owner, and its current status.
- A common scoring method multiplies likelihood by impact, each rated on a scale such as 1–5, giving a score out of 25. A risk rated likelihood 3 and impact 4 scores 12. Teams often colour-code scores on a likelihood–impact matrix (green, amber, red).
- Standard responses: avoid (change the plan so the risk cannot occur), reduce or mitigate (lower its likelihood or impact, for example by ordering spare components or testing early), transfer (pass it to someone else, as with insurance or a supplier warranty), and accept (live with low-scoring risks, ideally with a contingency plan).
- In EEE projects, typical risks include component failure or late delivery, software or firmware bugs found late, integration problems between subsystems, electrical safety hazards, and a team member being unavailable.
- Distinguish project risks (things that threaten the schedule or deliverables) from safety hazards (things that could hurt someone), which are handled by a risk assessment with control measures.

Exam or report tips: when you present a Gantt chart, identify the critical path and milestones; when you present a risk register, show that scores drove action and that the register was reviewed during the project, not written once and forgotten.

Engineering design produces several possible concepts, and the team must choose between them in a way that is transparent and defensible. A decision matrix structures that choice.

Weighted decision matrix
1. List the criteria that matter, drawn from the requirements (for example cost, ease of use, input/output capability, power consumption, safety, time to build).
2. Give each criterion a weight reflecting its importance. Weights are often chosen to sum to 1 (or 100%).
3. Score each option against each criterion on a fixed scale (for example 1–5), using evidence where possible.
4. Multiply each score by its weight and sum to give each option's weighted total.
5. Choose the highest total, then sanity-check the result: would a small change in a weight change the winner (a sensitivity check)?

Worked example (choosing a development board)
- Weights: cost 0.3, ease of use 0.2, I/O capability 0.3, power consumption 0.2.
- Option X scores 4, 5, 3, 3: total 0.3×4 + 0.2×5 + 0.3×3 + 0.2×3 = 3.7.
- Option Y scores 3, 3, 5, 4: total 0.9 + 0.6 + 1.5 + 0.8 = 3.8.
- Option Z scores 5, 4, 2, 3: total 1.5 + 0.8 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 3.5.
- Unweighted, X and Y tie on 15 points; weighting the criteria separates them and Y wins, because it is strong on a heavily weighted criterion. The margin is small, so the team should check the sensitivity and record the reasoning.

Pugh matrix (concept selection against a datum)
- Choose one concept (or an existing design) as the datum. For each criterion, mark every other concept as better (+), the same (S or 0) or worse (−) than the datum. Sum the pluses and minuses.
- It is quick and good for early concepts when detailed scores would be guesswork, and it often prompts hybrid concepts combining the strengths of several options.

Pitfalls
- Criteria that overlap (for example "cost" and "affordability") double-count one factor.
- Weights chosen after scoring, to justify a favourite, defeat the purpose.
- A must-have requirement (for example a safety rule) should be a pass/fail filter applied before scoring, not a weighted criterion that a high score elsewhere could outweigh.

Report tip: include the matrix, explain where the weights and scores came from, and state what you would need to change for a different option to win.

notes.h: Teamwork, technical writing and professional conduct
notes.body:
Scenario weeks and design projects are team efforts written up in reports and presentations, and the IEP's professional skills syllabus also covers ethics and professional standards.

Teamwork models
- Tuckman's model of group development (1965) has four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing; a fifth stage, adjourning, was added with Jensen in 1977. Expect some conflict (storming) early in a project, and agree ground rules to move through it.
- Belbin's team roles describe behaviour that people tend to show in teams (for example Coordinator, Shaper, Plant, Implementer, Completer Finisher). A balanced team covers the roles needed, whoever plays them.
- Practical habits: agree roles and responsibilities at the start, set SMART objectives (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound), keep short minutes of meetings with action points and owners, and raise problems early.

Technical report structure (a common pattern; follow your brief if it differs)
- Title and summary (or abstract): what was done, the key results and the main conclusion, readable on its own.
- Introduction: the problem, the requirements and the scope.
- Design or method: the concepts considered, how the choice was made (for example a decision matrix) and the final design, with circuit diagrams and block diagrams.
- Results and testing: what was measured and how, presented in labelled figures and tables with units.
- Discussion: whether requirements were met, sources of error, limitations and improvements.
- Conclusions: short answers to the questions set in the introduction.
- References: cited consistently in a recognised style; IEEE numeric referencing is common in electronic engineering.
- Writing style: write for your audience, define terms and acronyms, refer to every figure in the text, and keep one idea per paragraph.

Professional conduct
- In the UK, professional registration (for example as an Incorporated or Chartered Engineer) is overseen by the Engineering Council and awarded through licensed institutions; for electrical and electronic engineers this is typically the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET).
- The Statement of Ethical Principles published by the Engineering Council and the Royal Academy of Engineering was updated in February 2026 and now sets out five principles: honesty and integrity; responsibility to society; accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication; and responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment. The fifth principle is new and covers developing technologies such as AI responsibly, including their long-term effects. Older textbooks and websites quote the 2017 version, which had four principles (the second was worded as respect for life, law, the environment and public good).
- In student projects these appear as honest reporting of results (including failures), proper citation, safe working with electrical equipment, and considering sustainability and the wider effects of a design.

questions.q: A project has tasks A (3 days); B (2 days, after A); C (4 days, after A); and D (2 days, after both B and C). What is the minimum project duration?
questions.why: The paths are A–B–D (7 days) and A–C–D (9 days); the longest, A–C–D, is the critical path, so the project needs 9 days. 11 days adds every task in sequence, ignoring that B and C can run in parallel. 7 days follows the shorter path through B, but D cannot start until C has also finished. 4 days is just the longest single task, ignoring dependencies.

questions.q: A team arranges for a component supplier to replace any faulty boards free of charge under warranty. Which risk response is this?
questions.why: Passing the consequence of a risk to another party, here the supplier, is transfer. Avoiding would mean changing the plan so the risk cannot arise, such as not using that board at all. Accepting would mean taking no action beyond perhaps a contingency plan. Reducing would mean lowering the likelihood or impact yourselves, for example by testing boards on arrival or holding spares.

questions.q: Criteria weights are cost 0.3, ease of use 0.2, I/O capability 0.3 and power consumption 0.2. An option scores 3, 3, 5 and 4 respectively (out of 5). What is its weighted score?
questions.why: Weighted score = 0.3×3 + 0.2×3 + 0.3×5 + 0.2×4 = 0.9 + 0.6 + 1.5 + 0.8 = 3.8. 3.75 is the simple average of the four scores, which ignores the weights. 15 is the unweighted sum. 380 uses the weights as percentages (30, 20, 30, 20) without dividing by 100, so it is not on the 0–5 scale.

questions.q: In Tuckman's model of group development, which stage follows forming?
questions.why: The sequence is forming, storming, norming, performing (with adjourning added in 1977). Norming comes after storming, once the group has worked through early conflict. Performing is the stage of effective, productive work that follows norming. Adjourning is the final stage, when the team disbands at the end of the project.

questions.q: Explain how a weighted decision matrix is used to choose between design concepts, and give two ways a team could misuse it.
markScheme: Criteria from the requirements, each given a weight reflecting importance (1 mark)
Each option scored per criterion; weighted total = Σ weight × score; highest wins (1 mark)
Sensitivity check / record reasoning for weights and scores (1 mark)
Two misuses, e.g. overlapping criteria double-counting, weights chosen after scoring to favour a preferred option, or treating a must-have requirement as a weighted criterion (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: The team lists criteria taken from the requirements and gives each a weight (often summing to 1) reflecting how important it is. Each concept is scored against each criterion on a fixed scale, the scores are multiplied by the weights and summed, and the concept with the highest total is preferred. A sensitivity check, seeing whether small changes in weights change the winner, shows how robust the choice is, and the reasons for weights and scores should be recorded. It can be misused by choosing or adjusting weights after scoring to justify a favourite option, by including overlapping criteria that count the same factor twice, or by giving a must-have requirement (such as a safety rule) a weight instead of using it as a pass/fail filter.
